title: React Server Components
subtitle: React for two computers
throughline: One UI tree as it crosses the wire from the server to the browser, and one form submission that crosses back.

chapters.title: React for Two Computers
chapters.blurb: Why RSC serializes the React tree itself across the network instead of shipping HTML.

steps.title: React for Two Computers
steps.narration: A React app is really **one program running on two computers**. Server Components run where the data lives; Client Components run where the user clicks. *React Server Components* is the protocol that lets one tree span both.
steps.say: Here is the idea that makes everything else click. A React app is really one program running on two computers. Some of it runs on the server, near the data. Some of it runs in the browser, near the user. React Server Components is how a single tree spans both.
steps.coverSubtitle: One program, split across a server and a browser

steps.title: A tree across two machines
steps.narration: A **Server Component** can read a database or a secret directly — it never reaches the browser. The **browser** still needs an interactive tree to paint. The whole problem is getting one across the gap to the other.
steps.say: A Server Component runs only on the server, so it can read a database or a secret directly, and its code never reaches the browser. But the browser still needs a tree to paint. The whole problem is getting from one machine to the other.

steps.title: Serialize the tree, not HTML
steps.narration: The naive answer is to render **HTML** — but HTML is dead text; it loses which components are which. Instead the server hands its tree to the **Flight serializer**, `renderToReadableStream` in `ReactFlightServer`.
steps.say: The naive answer is to render HTML and send that. But HTML is dead text. It forgets which components were which, so the browser can never reconnect the interactive parts. Instead, the server hands its live tree to the Flight serializer.

steps.title: A stream of rows
steps.narration: Flight writes the tree as a **stream of numbered rows** — each row is `id:tag` plus a payload, ended by a newline. It is the React tree itself, serialized, not markup.
steps.say: Flight does not produce a page. It produces a stream of numbered rows. Each row is an id, a tag letter, and a payload, ended by a newline. Taken together, the rows are the React tree itself, serialized, streaming out as it renders.

steps.title: The browser reads the stream
steps.narration: In the browser, the **Flight client** — `createFromReadableStream` in `ReactFlightClient` — consumes those rows as they arrive, without waiting for the whole response.
steps.say: On the other computer, the Flight client reads that stream. It consumes the rows as they arrive, building structure incrementally, never waiting for the whole response before it can start.

steps.title: Rebuild and paint
steps.narration: From the rows the client reconstructs the same **React element tree** the server described, and React paints it into the **browser**.
steps.say: From those rows the client rebuilds the exact element tree the server described, and React paints it into the page. The tree the server imagined now lives in the browser.

steps.title: The one-way path
steps.narration: End to end: **server tree** → **Flight serializer** → **rows** → **Flight client** → **browser**. One tree, two computers, a stream in between.
steps.say: So here is the whole one way path. The server tree is serialized by Flight into rows, the rows stream across, the Flight client rebuilds the tree, and the browser paints it. One tree, two computers, a stream in between. Now let us look closely at what those rows actually say.

chapters.title: The Flight Wire Format
chapters.blurb: How one value becomes numbered rows, outlined references, and $-prefixed sentinels — then comes back to life.

steps.title: The Flight Wire Format
steps.narration: Flight is mostly **JSON with a grammar on top**. Each row is `id:tag` plus a payload; values that recur or arrive late are *outlined* to their own row and pointed at by reference. This is that grammar.
steps.say: The wire format looks like J S O N, but with a small grammar layered on top. Each row is numbered, values that repeat or arrive late get their own row, and a handful of special markers carry the things J S O N can't. Let us walk through it.

steps.title: Every row is id, tag, payload
steps.narration: **`renderModelDestructive`** serializes a value and **`emitModelChunk`** writes the row: the id in hex, a tag, the payload, a newline. A plain model row is just `id:` then JSON.
steps.say: Start on the server. The serializer walks a value and writes a row for it. The row is the id in hexadecimal, a colon, an optional tag letter, then the payload, then a newline. A plain model row is just an id, a colon, and its J S O N.

steps.title: The tag names the kind
steps.narration: The tag picks the row's kind: no tag is a **model**, `I` is an **import** (a client reference), `E` an **error**, `H` a **hint**, `T` a text blob. One stream multiplexes them all by id.
steps.say: That tag letter is how one stream carries many kinds of thing. No tag means an ordinary model. An I row is an import, a pointer to client code. An E row is an error. An H row is a preloading hint. Every row is addressed by its id, so they can arrive in any order.

steps.title: Shared values get outlined
steps.narration: When a value is shared, async, or large, **`outlineModel`** gives it its *own* numbered row and leaves a reference behind — `serializeByValueID` writes `$` + the row id in hex.
steps.say: Now the clever part. When a value is shared, or large, or not ready yet, the serializer outlines it. It writes that value as its own numbered row, and in the original spot it leaves a tiny reference: a dollar sign followed by the row id. The graph is flattened into rows that point at each other.

steps.title: Dollar-sign sentinels
steps.narration: Types JSON can't hold ride as **`$`-sentinels**: `$@` a Promise, `$L` a lazy node, `$D` a Date, `$undefined`, `$Infinity`. A real string starting with `$` is escaped to `$$`.
steps.say: The same dollar sign trick carries the types plain J S O N can't hold. A dollar-at is a promise. A dollar-L is a lazy node. There are markers for dates, for undefined, for infinity, even for negative zero. And if your actual string happens to start with a dollar sign, it is escaped by doubling it, so nothing is mistaken for a marker.

steps.title: The client walks the JSON
steps.narration: In the browser, **`parseModelString`** is the reviver: as `JSON.parse` walks each row, every string is inspected for a leading `$`.
steps.say: Cross to the browser. As the Flight client parses each row, it runs a reviver over every string. That reviver, parse model string, is where the grammar is undone. If a string starts with a dollar sign, it is not data, it is an instruction.

steps.title: References become live objects
steps.narration: Each marker is rehydrated: `$` + id resolves another row via `getChunk`, `$@` becomes a real **Promise**, `$L` a lazy wrapper, `$S` a Symbol — yielding a **live JS value**, not text.
steps.say: Each marker is turned back into the real thing. A plain reference looks up another chunk by id. A dollar-at becomes an actual promise the UI can suspend on. A dollar-L becomes a lazy wrapper. A dollar-S becomes a symbol. What comes out the other side is a living JavaScript value, with its sharing and its promises intact.

steps.title: Flatten, stream, rebuild
steps.narration: A value graph is flattened to rows, references and `$`-sentinels stream across, and **`parseModelString`** rebuilds the same graph — promises and all — on the far computer.
steps.say: That is the whole format. A value graph is flattened into numbered rows, the cross-links become tiny references, the awkward types become dollar markers, and on the far side the reviver rebuilds the very same graph. Next, the most interesting reference of all: a pointer to code on the other machine.

chapters.title: use client — The Door to the Browser
chapters.blurb: How a "use client" boundary becomes an Import row and a $L pointer that the bundler resolves in the browser.

story.title: use client — The Door to the Browser
story.subtitle: React for two computers

steps.title: use client — The Door to the Browser
steps.narration: A **`"use client"`** module marks a door between the two computers. The server never serializes that component's *code* — only a **reference** the browser knows how to resolve.
steps.say: A use client directive marks a door between the two computers. When the server tree reaches one of those components, it does something subtle. It never sends the component's code. It sends only a reference to it, and trusts the browser to find the real thing.
steps.coverSubtitle: The server ships a pointer to code, never the code

steps.title: The tree hits a client boundary
steps.narration: While serializing, the server meets a **Client Reference** — a `"use client"` module the bundler has tagged. `serializeClientReference` handles it specially.
steps.say: As the server serializes its tree, it meets a client reference: a module the bundler tagged with use client. That component can't run on the server at all. So the serializer takes a different path for it.

steps.title: It emits an Import row
steps.narration: **`emitImportChunk`** writes an `id:I` row whose payload is the **client reference metadata** — the chunk ids and export name. In the tree, a `$L` lazy pointer takes the component's place.
steps.say: Instead of code, the server emits an import row, tagged with the letter I. Its payload is the client reference metadata: which bundle chunks to load and which export to use. And where the component sat in the tree, the server leaves a lazy pointer, so React knows something will load there later.

steps.title: The client reads the I row
steps.narration: In the browser, **`resolveModule`** in `ReactFlightClient` parses the metadata out of the `I` row.
steps.say: The import row streams to the browser. There, resolve module pulls the client reference metadata back out of it. The browser now knows the identity of a component it has not yet loaded.

steps.title: Resolve against the manifest
steps.narration: **`resolveClientReference`** looks the metadata up in the **bundler manifest** (`moduleMap` / `bundlerConfig`) to find the actual chunk URL and export.
steps.say: The metadata is just an identity, not a location. So resolve client reference looks it up in the bundler's manifest, the module map that maps each reference to a real chunk on disk and a named export. This is the one piece the framework's bundler must supply.

steps.title: Load and mount the real thing
steps.narration: **`preloadModule`** fetches the chunk, **`requireModule`** pulls the export, and React resolves the `$L` lazy — so the **real Client Component** mounts and becomes interactive.
steps.say: Now the browser preloads that chunk and requires the export. The lazy pointer left in the tree resolves to the real client component, and React mounts it. The reference has become running, interactive code, exactly where the server said it would be.

steps.title: A reference, resolved
steps.narration: Server **boundary** → `I` **row** → **client** → **manifest** → **mounted component**. The network became the module boundary; the bundler is the only glue.
steps.say: So a use client boundary travels as a reference, not as code. An import row crosses the wire, the client resolves it against the bundler manifest, loads the chunk, and mounts the real component. The network itself became the module boundary. Now let us run that door in reverse.

chapters.title: use server — The Call Back
chapters.blurb: How a Server Action becomes a $ACTION_ID reference, encodeReply ships the args, and decodeAction runs it.

steps.title: use server — The Call Back
steps.narration: A **`"use server"`** function handed to the client is not the function — it is an **id**. Calling it ships the arguments back over the wire, and the server runs the real thing.
steps.say: Now the same trick in the other direction. A use server function can be handed to the browser, but what the browser holds is not the function. It is an id. Calling it sends the arguments back to the server, where the real function runs.
steps.coverSubtitle: A function on the client that runs on the server

steps.title: The client holds a stand-in
steps.narration: On the client, **`createServerReference(id, callServer)`** returns a function whose whole body is `callServer(id, args)`. It is a stand-in for code that lives on the server.
steps.say: On the client, create server reference builds that stand-in. The function it returns has almost no body. All it does is call back to the server with its id and whatever arguments it was given. The browser can pass it around like any function, but it is really a remote handle.

steps.title: Encode the arguments
steps.narration: **`encodeReply` / `processReply`** serialize the arguments — the same Flight grammar in reverse — into a **`FormData`** body. Blobs and files become real parts; the action itself is named by `$ACTION_ID_`.
steps.say: Calling it runs encode reply. This is the wire format we just learned, but going the other way: the arguments are serialized into form data. Files and blobs become real multipart fields so they can stream. And the action being invoked is named by an action id field.

steps.title: Post it to the server
steps.narration: The reply is POSTed back. On the server, **`decodeAction`** in `ReactFlightActionServer` walks the `FormData`, finding `$ACTION_ID_` or `$ACTION_REF_` fields.
steps.say: The form data is posted back to the server. There, decode action walks every field. The fields that don't start with action underscore are the real form inputs. The ones that do identify which server function to run, and carry any arguments that were bound to it ahead of time.

steps.title: Resolve the id to a module
steps.narration: **`loadServerReference`** calls **`resolveServerReference(serverManifest, id)`** — the server's own manifest maps the id to a real module, mirroring the client manifest from before.
steps.say: The id is meaningless on its own, so the server looks it up in its own manifest. Resolve server reference maps that id to a real module on the server, exactly mirroring how the client resolved a component a moment ago. Each computer keeps a manifest for the other's references.

steps.title: Bind the args and run
steps.narration: **`requireModule`** loads the function, **`bindArgs(fn, args)`** prepends any bound arguments, and the action runs with the remaining `FormData` — under a `MAX_BOUND_ARGS` guard.
steps.say: With the module in hand, the server requires the function, binds any arguments that travelled with the reference, and calls it with the rest of the form data. A limit on bound arguments keeps a hostile client from forcing huge calls. The function the browser only held a handle to has finally run, on the server.

steps.title: Stream the result back
steps.narration: The return value is serialized as **Flight** and streamed to the browser; **`useActionState`** and `decodeFormState` thread it back into the form as new state.
steps.say: And the answer comes home the way everything else does, as a Flight stream. The return value is serialized and sent back, and use action state threads it into the form as the new state. The round trip is closed: a click in the browser became a function call on the server and a fresh piece of UI in return.

steps.title: The reply round trip
steps.narration: **form** → `createServerReference` → `encodeReply` → `decodeAction` → `resolveServerReference` → **run** → Flight result. References point both ways across the wire.
steps.say: So a server action is the mirror image of a client component. One is a reference to code that runs in the browser, the other a reference to code that runs on the server. Same wire format, same manifest idea, pointing in opposite directions. Let us see the whole loop at once.

chapters.title: The Round Trip
chapters.blurb: The whole picture: render down to the browser, act back up to the server, and re-render — one program on two computers.

steps.title: The Round Trip
steps.narration: Put it together: a tree renders **down** to the browser as Flight, an action travels **back up** to the server, and the server **re-renders**. One program, two computers, looping.
steps.say: Let us put the whole thing together. A tree renders down to the browser as Flight. An action travels back up to the server. The server re-renders and streams down again. One program, two computers, in a loop.
steps.coverSubtitle: Render down, act back up, re-render

steps.title: Two computers, one program
steps.narration: On the left, the **server** runs Server Components near the data. On the right, the **browser** runs the interactive tree near the user. Everything else is how they talk.
steps.say: On the left is the server, running components close to the data. On the right is the browser, running the interactive parts close to the user. Everything in between is just how these two halves of one program talk to each other.

steps.title: Render down as Flight
steps.narration: **`renderToReadableStream`** hands the tree to **`ReactFlightServer`**, which emits the `id:tag` **rows** of the RSC stream.
steps.say: The trip starts on the server. Render to readable stream hands the tree to the Flight serializer, which writes it out as the numbered rows of the R S C stream, flowing as it renders.

steps.title: Rebuild in the browser
steps.narration: The **Flight client** parses the rows — resolving client references against the manifest — and mounts the **browser UI**.
steps.say: The Flight client reads those rows, resolves each client reference against the bundler manifest, and mounts the interactive tree in the browser. The picture the server described is now live in front of the user.

steps.title: An action goes back up
steps.narration: The user submits a form. **`encodeReply`** packs the arguments into a **`FormData`** reply addressed by `$ACTION_ID_`.
steps.say: Then the user acts. They submit a form, or call a server function. Encode reply packs the arguments into a form data body, tagged with the id of the action to run, and sends it back up to the server.

steps.title: Run, then re-render
steps.narration: **`decodeAction`** resolves the id and runs the **Server Action**; its result feeds a fresh render — which streams **down** again, closing the loop.
steps.say: On the server, decode action resolves that id and runs the real function. Its result feeds a fresh render, and the new tree streams down the very same way. The loop is closed, and it can turn again and again.

steps.title: References are the seam
steps.narration: Both directions ride one idea: **code stays put, references travel**. A client reference points into the browser; a server reference points into the server. The wire format carries both.
steps.say: Notice the single idea underneath both directions. Code never moves. References do. A client reference points from the server into the browser. A server reference points from the browser into the server. The same little wire format carries both, and that seam is the whole architecture.

steps.title: The whole loop
steps.narration: **server** → **Flight** → **wire** → **client** → **browser** → **reply** → **action** → **server**. React, stretched across two computers and folded into a loop.
steps.say: So this is React Server Components, end to end. The server renders, Flight serializes, the stream crosses, the client rebuilds, the browser paints, an action replies, the server runs it and renders again. React, stretched across two computers and folded into a single loop.
